questions.prompt: Match each API style or artifact.
questions.explanation: REST is resource-oriented and human-readable; gRPC is efficient for service-to-service calls; OpenAPI documents contracts.

concept_panel.title: REST vs gRPC
concept_panel.explanation: REST usually exposes resources over HTTP with JSON and is easy for humans and browsers to inspect. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 and is often better for internal service-to-service APIs where generated clients and efficient binary payloads matter. The right answer depends on consumers, tooling, latency, and operability. Public APIs often favor REST; internal low-latency services may favor gRPC.
key_takeaways: REST is resource-oriented and easy to inspect.
gRPC is contract-first and efficient for internal services.
Generated clients reduce drift but add tooling requirements.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can choose API styles based on clients and operational constraints.
concept_panel.practical_example: A mobile app public API may use REST, while checkout and inventory services communicate with gRPC internally.

questions.prompt: What belongs in an API contract?
questions.explanation: An API contract defines how client and server communicate: routes, parameters, payloads, response shapes, and status behavior.

concept_panel.title: API Contracts and OpenAPI
concept_panel.explanation: An API contract defines endpoints, inputs, outputs, status codes, and error shapes. OpenAPI is a machine-readable way to describe that contract, and Swagger UI is a common interface for exploring it. Contracts let frontend and backend teams work independently. Breaking changes should be versioned or rolled out carefully.
key_takeaways: Contracts define request and response expectations.
OpenAPI documents contracts in a structured format.
Swagger UI is a viewer, not the contract itself.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand API reliability and client/server coordination.
concept_panel.practical_example: FastAPI generates `/docs` from the OpenAPI schema so clients can inspect available endpoints.

questions.explanation: Offset is easy for dashboards; cursor is safer for large or changing feeds.

pairs.right: Simple page numbers but unstable on changing data
Continue after a stable record marker

answer.Offset pagination: Simple page numbers but unstable on changing data
answer.Cursor pagination: Continue after a stable record marker

concept_panel.title: Cursor vs Offset Pagination
concept_panel.explanation: Offset pagination skips a number of rows and is simple for stable datasets. Cursor pagination continues from a stable record marker, which is safer when rows are inserted or deleted while the user pages. Large offsets can also become expensive because the database still has to walk past skipped rows. Feeds and timelines usually prefer cursors.
key_takeaways: Offset is simple but unstable on changing data.
Cursor pagination follows a stable position.
Cursor pagination usually fits large feeds better.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand API data access patterns at scale.
concept_panel.practical_example: A feed ordered by created_at can use the last seen timestamp/id as the next cursor.

questions.prompt: Which requests are idempotent in normal REST design?
questions.explanation: Idempotent operations produce the same final state when repeated. POST usually creates another resource unless protected by an idempotency key.

concept_panel.title: Idempotency Keys
concept_panel.explanation: An idempotent operation can be repeated without changing the final result beyond the first attempt. POST is often not idempotent because it creates a new resource each time. If a payment request times out, the server may still have processed it; retrying without an idempotency key can charge twice. Idempotency keys let the server recognize a retry and return the original result.
key_takeaways: Timeout does not prove failure.
POST retries can duplicate work.
Idempotency keys make unsafe retries safer.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand API reliability under partial failure.
concept_panel.practical_example: POST /payments with Idempotency-Key: abc123 can return the first payment response when the client retries.

coding_challenges.title: APIs status classifier
coding_challenges.instructions: Implement classify_status_code(code: int) -> str. Return success for 200-299, redirect for 300-399, client_error for 400-499, server_error for 500-599, and unknown otherwise.
coding_challenges.explanation: The challenge reinforces deterministic branching, status-code categories, and local test execution.
